1.pericope_label: Now the word of the Lord came unto Jonah the son of Amittai, saying,

schools.summary: Ellicott grants that the opening particle is strictly 'And' but holds that the received English adequately represents the ordinary Hebrew way of beginning a narrative; Keil and Delitzsch supply the man, born at Gath-hepher in Zebulon, living under the second Jeroboam and having foretold that king's success, and argue from the identical patronymic that the prophet of the earlier oracle and the man commissioned here are one, the eastern mission falling later.

Gill treats the particle as a conversive rather than a copulative, turning future into past, and denies that the opening implies any lost fragment, since Hebrew historical books commonly begin so; Calvin presses the same particle further, taking it to intimate that the man was already in the teaching office, and finds the purpose of the mission in shaming a people who despised every prophet sent them while a heathen city turned in three days.

Clarke gives the biography and the chronology, then closes the question of genre: rehearsing the allegorical, mythological and parabolic expedients, he sets against them our Lord's appeal to the main facts and undertakes the book in its literal sense alone.

Henry reads the commission as an honour, finding significance in the names, the dove and 'my truth', and insisting that the word came to the prophet, was to him, since God's words are substance where the words of men are wind.

debates.question: What does the opening particle imply?

positions.position: Nothing beyond the ordinary Hebrew manner of opening a narrative; no earlier matter is presupposed.
That the man was already a prophet in office, so that this commission continues a function rather than beginning one.

outliers.claim: Sets a Phoenician fable of Hesione, rescued by Hercules from a sea-monster and quoted from Lycophron and the scholiasts, beside the history, judging that the fable was more likely borrowed from the history than the reverse, and declares that our Lord's appeal to the facts puts an end to all mythological, allegorical and hypothetical interpretation.

themes: Now the word of the Lord came unto Jonah the son of Amittai, saying,

2.pericope_label: Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and cry against it; for their wickedness is come up before me. But Jonah rose up to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the Lord, and went down to Joppa; and he found a ship going to Tarshish: so he paid the fare thereof, and went down into it, to go with them unto Tarshish from the presence of the Lord.

schools.summary: Ellicott points to the mounds along the Tigris as more than confirming the ancient impression of the city's size, and takes what lies beneath them to be less a city than a group of cities; Keil and Delitzsch identify the port of flight as Tartessus in Spain and read the phrase about the divine presence as withdrawal from the service of the God-King of Israel and from the land where he manifested himself, not as concealment from an omnipresent God.

Gill sets out the city's antiquity and founder and canvasses the candidates for the port, inclining to Tarsus in Cilicia; Calvin asks why the greatness is mentioned and answers that it was spoken to arm the prophet against terror, distinguishes this mission from that of Nahum, who prophesied against the same city from home and for the comfort of a distressed people, and traces the flight to novelty, doubt of any fruit, and the weakness of the flesh.

Clarke reports the measurements with caution, allows that the circuit took in cultivated ground, and finds in the wickedness that comes up a personification of evil ascending to stand before the Supreme Judge and witness against its own delinquency.

debates.question: Where was the port of flight?

positions.position: Tartessus in Spain, on the Guadalquivir.
Tarsus in Cilicia, on the authority of Josephus and Saadiah Gaon.
Cilicia, but as a country rather than a city, and certainly not the sea itself.

outliers.claim: Holds that the epithet 'great' was given for the prophet's sake rather than the reader's, to arm him beforehand against the splendour, wealth and power that would otherwise have frightened him out of the errand.

themes: Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and cry against it; for their wickedness is come up before me.

But Jonah rose up to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the Lord, and went down to Joppa; and he found a ship going to Tarshish: so he paid the fare thereof, and went down into it, to go with them unto Tarshish from the presence of the Lord.

4.pericope_label: But the Lord sent out a great wind into the sea, and there was a mighty tempest in the sea, so that the ship was like to be broken.

schools.summary: Ellicott hears in the verb the sudden burst of a squall on a coast sailors knew to be dangerous, and finds in the clause about the ship a seaman's way of speaking, to whom his vessel is a living thing with feelings, hopes and fears; Keil and Delitzsch render it as a throwing of a great wind upon the sea and treat the ship's 'thinking' as an idiom used of lifeless things, amounting to 'was very nearly wrecked'.

Gill takes the wind out of God's treasures and stresses that it was hurled into that part of the sea where the ship was riding, in pursuit of a man who thought himself clear away; Calvin refuses all chance, deriving the verb from a root implying force, and meets the objection that many suffered for one by arguing that God may justly involve others, humbling some and chastising or trying others in the same stroke.
Clarke is brief: a storm which, as the sequel shows, came by God's immediate direction, and under which they had nearly suffered shipwreck.

Henry reads the storm as a pursuer sent after a deserter, notes that the wind blows where it wills as far as we are concerned but where God directs as far as he is concerned, observes that the clause may single out that ship and no other, and turns the tempest into mercy, since it was sent to fetch a runaway home.

debates.question: How should the clause about the ship thinking itself broken be construed?

positions.position: As an idiom applied to lifeless things, equivalent to 'was very nearly wrecked'.
As a sailor's personification, the vessel being to him a living thing with hopes and fears.
Some make the ship a metonymy for the mariners, but the plainer construction is to be kept, common speech agreeing at many points with the Hebrew.

outliers.claim: Turns one storm into a general rule of providence, that no change in the air, no rain and no tempest at sea happens by chance, and answers the charge of injustice by arguing that God may punish one man so as at the same time to humble some, chastise others and try the patience of yet others.

themes: But the Lord sent out a great wind into the sea, and there was a mighty tempest in the sea, so that the ship was like to be broken.

5.pericope_label: Then the mariners were afraid, and cried every man unto his god, and cast forth the wares that were in the ship into the sea, to lighten it of them. But Jonah was gone down into the sides of the ship; and he lay, and was fast asleep. So the shipmaster came to him, and said unto him, What meanest thou, O sleeper? arise, call upon thy God, if so be that God will think upon us, that we perish not.

schools.summary: Ellicott works through the vocabulary, taking the jettisoned goods as movables of every sort while the cargo proper would be kept till the last extremity, preferring 'recesses' to 'sides', and deriving the word for the vessel from a root meaning to cover with boards, so that a decked ship is meant; Keil and Delitzsch name the officer the upper-steersman, chief of those who manage the ship, and note that the divine name in his appeal carries the article and so means the true God.

Gill argues from the crew's terror that the storm was supernatural, men bred to the sea not being easily frightened, and identifies the officer as master of the ropers; Calvin draws the same inference from their fear, enumerates the circumstances as a portrait of the sleeper's insensibility, and turns the appeal to pray into an indictment of religion without a rule, since men content with a general apprehension of God each shape a deity to their own fancy.

Clarke takes the crew for heathens each with a different object of worship, reads the jettison as lading thrown over to ride out the weather, pictures berths below deck like those of our packets, and explains the deep sleep as exhaustion following distress, recalling the disciples in the garden.

debates.question: How is the prophet's sleep to be explained?

positions.position: Fatigue after a hurried flight, together with the quiet that follows an irrevocable resolution, before remorse begins.
Exhaustion and distress, which in many cases terminate in heavy sleep.
Culpable insensibility: a man carrying his own executioner in his heart ought to have trembled even asleep.

outliers.claim: Makes the shipmaster's inability to bind his passenger to any particular worship the occasion of a general argument, that without a certain rule of religion there is no stability, all agreeing that there is some God while in the particulars every one invents a crooked path and is left wandering in a labyrinth.

themes: Then the mariners were afraid, and cried every man unto his god, and cast forth the wares that were in the ship into the sea, to lighten it of them. But Jonah was gone down into the sides of the ship; and he lay, and was fast asleep.
So the shipmaster came to him, and said unto him, What meanest thou, O sleeper? arise, call upon thy God, if so be that God will think upon us, that we perish not.

7.pericope_label: And they said every one to his fellow, Come, and let us cast lots, that we may know for whose cause this evil is upon us. So they cast lots, and the lot fell upon Jonah. Then said they unto him, Tell us, we pray thee, for whose cause this evil is upon us; What is thine occupation? and whence comest thou? what is thy country? and of what people art thou?

schools.summary: Ellicott sets the resort to lots among the classical and scriptural instances of the belief that an impious passenger draws his companions into ruin, quoting the ode that bars such a man from house and voyage, and finds artistry in the grammar of the questions, the idiom being put more elegantly to the prophet than the sailors had used it among themselves, with the repetition natural in men who want a verdict confirmed from the offender's mouth.

Gill notes that they did not fall upon him at once but treated him with respect, tenderness and lenity; Calvin takes the proposal itself as proof that the tempest was no ordinary one, since lots are not the usual expedient when weather rises but the recourse of men destitute of judgment, and holds that two convictions were operating even in heathens, that God draws out truth and that he presides over what seems most fortuitous.

Clarke calls the practice a very ancient way of seeking the mind of Divine Providence, illustrates the sailors' state of mind with the story of the philosopher who told a praying crew to be silent lest the gods learn he was aboard, and holds that in this instance God directed the lot; on the questioning he finds a very gentle method of bringing the charge home.

Henry draws the moral of the scene, that those who profess religion will hear of their wrongdoing from people who make no such profession, and that when sin has raised a storm the question that matters is what is to be done with the sin that raised it.

outliers.claim: Holds that the sailors were partly in error even as they cast the lot, since the practice belongs to men who have lost judgment and counsel, and yet that God overruled it, so that the same act is at once a mark of extreme fear and an instrument of divine disclosure.

themes: And they said every one to his fellow, Come, and let us cast lots, that we may know for whose cause this evil is upon us. So they cast lots, and the lot fell upon Jonah.
Then said they unto him, Tell us, we pray thee, for whose cause this evil is upon us; What is thine occupation? and whence comest thou? what is thy country? and of what people art thou?

9.pericope_label: And he said unto them, I am an Hebrew; and I fear the Lord, the God of heaven, which hath made the sea and the dry land. Then were the men exceedingly afraid, and said unto him, Why hast thou done this? For the men knew that he fled from the presence of the Lord, because he had told them.

schools.summary: Ellicott notes that the original order is more striking, a Hebrew I, that the Greek translators read a servant of the Lord, and that the recorded reply abbreviates what was said; he takes the confession of the Creator as spoken for the crew, who owned the God of Israel as a tribal deity but never as maker of the world they lived in, and insists that their question expresses horror rather than curiosity. Keil and Delitzsch put the effect simply as fearing, in the storm, the wrath of God on account of the prophet's sin.

Gill explains why the older name was chosen, since Jew would have been false and Israelite would have implied that people's idolatries, and traces the crew's terror to their reasoning that if flight was punished so, worse offenders had worse to fear; Calvin observes that the answer reverses the order of the questions, argues that naming the true God first aggravates rather than excuses the offence, and reads their great fear as a serious dread that gave God his glory, unlike the alarms with which superstitious men cajole themselves.

Clarke calls this the point at which the man was faithful, giving honest testimony to the God he served and setting him before the sailors far above the objects of their own adoration, the God of heaven who made sea and dry land and governs both.

debates.question: How does the confession bear on the prophet's guilt?

positions.position: Favourably: the emergency recalls him to himself, and from here his conduct is dignified and manly.
As an aggravation: to begin with the framer of heaven, known to him, makes the flight monstrous rather than excusable.

outliers.claim: Finds a further justice in the reproof itself, that a man who withdrew from God's authority is now set beneath heathens and barbarians, who become his censors and judges.

themes: And he said unto them, I am an Hebrew; and I fear the Lord, the God of heaven, which hath made the sea and the dry land.
Then were the men exceedingly afraid, and said unto him, Why hast thou done this? For the men knew that he fled from the presence of the Lord, because he had told them.

11.pericope_label: Then said they unto him, What shall we do unto thee, that the sea may be calm unto us? for the sea wrought, and was tempestuous. And he said unto them, Take me up, and cast me forth into the sea; so shall the sea be calm unto you: for I know that for my sake this great tempest is upon you.

schools.summary: Ellicott observes that the word rendered calm is used of the lull after a storm and of peace after strife, that the phrase for the raging is literally that the sea was going and being agitated, and holds that no prophetic inspiration was needed for the sentence the prophet passes on himself, since he is simply too manly to survive at the cost of others.

Gill guards the motive from misconstruction, denying both that the man preferred death to the journey and the rabbinic suggestion that he had overheard a plan to throw him over, and insists that he must die by the hand of justice rather than leap in himself; Calvin traces the crew's restraint to the fear of God, is exact on the idiom that the sea may cease from upon them, and defends the prophet against the charge of despair, since he knew himself summoned by an unmistakable voice.
Clarke sums the crew up in a sentence, that in these poor men there was an uncommon degree of humanity and tender feeling.

Henry makes the continuing storm the point, since to find sin the cause of our troubles and not forsake it is to make bad worse, and commends the crew for consulting the offender, treating a delinquent who was also a penitent with the tenderness owed to those overtaken in a fault.

debates.question: Did the prophet's sentence on himself require prophetic inspiration?

positions.position: No: any man of that temper would prefer to perish rather than involve others in his ruin.
Yes: the knowledge could not come from the lot, which was common to all aboard, but from the prophetic spirit and his instruction in true religion.

outliers.claim: Passes on a striking if fanciful comment, that the sea went as commanded, went to manifest the vengeance of its Lord, went to prosecute a runaway prophet, and swelled into larger billows while the mariners delayed.

themes: Then said they unto him, What shall we do unto thee, that the sea may be calm unto us? for the sea wrought, and was tempestuous.
And he said unto them, Take me up, and cast me forth into the sea; so shall the sea be calm unto you: for I know that for my sake this great tempest is upon you.

13.pericope_label: Nevertheless the men rowed hard to bring it to the land; but they could not: for the sea wrought, and was tempestuous against them. Wherefore they cried unto the Lord, and said, We beseech thee, O Lord, we beseech thee, let us not perish for this man’s life, and lay not upon us innocent blood: for thou, O Lord, hast done as it pleased thee.

schools.summary: Ellicott recovers the metaphor buried in the verb, which everywhere else describes breaking through a wall, so that the picture is of forcing a vessel through the wave-wall, calls it a fine trait that the crew would not obey the request until every effort had been tried, and finds in their prayer the contrast running through the book between heathen readiness and the stubbornness of Israel, the storm, the lot and the prophet's own request showing them to be only instruments of a purpose not their own.

Gill observes that they cried not to their own gods but to the God of the Hebrews, of whom this providence had given them some knowledge, and that they prayed before laying a hand on the man; Calvin reads their reluctance as a change wrought in them, argues that it is not in our power to weigh sins since the balance is false when we judge our own, and draws from their appeal the rule that an abhorrence of cruelty is implanted by nature in every man.

Clarke reports their unwillingness to proceed to such an extremity, holds that they were now convinced of the self-existing Being who made heaven and earth and raised this storm, and reads their prayer as calling God to witness that they acted with the utmost reluctance and only in obedience.

Henry sets the rowing against wind and tide, the wind of God's displeasure and the tide of his counsel, holds it vain to think of saving ourselves by any means but destroying our sins, and adds that even natural conscience cannot but dread blood-guiltiness.

outliers.claim: Sets beside the sailors' plea a passage from the Argonautic poem in which a crew debate whether to kill the wretched Medea and cast her as prey to the fishes in order to avert their own fate.

themes: Nevertheless the men rowed hard to bring it to the land; but they could not: for the sea wrought, and was tempestuous against them.

Wherefore they cried unto the Lord, and said, We beseech thee, O Lord, we beseech thee, let us not perish for this man’s life, and lay not upon us innocent blood: for thou, O Lord, hast done as it pleased thee.

15.pericope_label: So they took up Jonah, and cast him forth into the sea: and the sea ceased from her raging. Then the men feared the Lord exceedingly, and offered a sacrifice unto the Lord, and made vows. Now the Lord had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.

schools.summary: Ellicott holds that the pluperfect misleads and the verb means appointed, the same word being used later of the gourd, the worm and the east wind, so that no prior preparation and still less a creature made for the occasion is implied; he notes the dragon of early Christian painting and warns that until the prior question of the book's kind is settled the whole disquisition about the fish looks vain and useless. Keil and Delitzsch date the sacrifice to the ship rather than the shore and identify the creature as a large shark, giving its length and its four hundred teeth in six rows.

Gill distinguishes the crew's new fear as religious rather than natural and reverential rather than servile, denies that the fish was formed at the creation for this office, reads the verb of a providence that brought it alongside, and notes that the Greek word rendered whale must cover all great fishes; Calvin argues that the instant calm proved the man condemned by God's own judgment, and refuses to read the crew's fear as a thorough conversion, holding that the Lord extorted a confession in the moment.

Clarke thinks the sacrifice perhaps the first ever offered aboard a vessel since the ark floated on the deluge and judges it most probable that these heathens became sincere converts; on the creature he rejects the whale, whose throat can scarcely admit a man's leg, and proposes the shark, common in that sea and known to swallow men thrown overboard.

positions.position: Most probably yes: seeing what was done, they became sincere converts to the true God.
Their fear was religious and reverential rather than servile, since they had seen both God's power and his goodness.
No thorough conversion: a confession was extorted in the moment, and if no progress followed, their knowledge only condemned them.
A shark or dog-fish, the whale's throat being too small.
The question cannot be settled, and is idle, until it is decided whether the book is literal history, an apologue or a parable.

outliers.claim: Turns from the creature to the man's state of mind, arguing that one cut off from the common light and from human society, by a punishment once reserved for parricides, underwent a continual execution rather than a death, and that no one can comprehend what passed through that mind.

themes: So they took up Jonah, and cast him forth into the sea: and the sea ceased from her raging.
Then the men feared the Lord exceedingly, and offered a sacrifice unto the Lord, and made vows.
Now the Lord had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.
